newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says Japan sees aid priority to Jakarta.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says Japan sees aid priority to Jakarta.

text.p: Indonesian Planning Minister Ginanjar Kartasasmita said on Friday Japan would continue supporting his country's development despite cutting its aid budget.
"The Japanese government told me it would make its foreign aid to Indonesia a priority despite cutting its foreign aid budget," Ginanjar told reporters after meeting President Suharto.
"I don't know how much Japan will give (but) we hope Japan will maintain the same level of aid to Indonesia," he said.
Ginanjar said Japan was cutting its global foreign aid in order to adjust its budget to the current demands of its economy.
He has said Indonesia expects to obtain some $5 billion in foreign aid this year and hoped its controversial national car policy would not hurt ties with key donor nations.
The funds will come from the World Bank-chaired Consultative Group for Indonesia (CGI), which consists of 20 donor countries, including Japan, and several financing agencies.
The CGI plans to meet next month in Japan.
The CGI pledged $5.26 billion in aid to Indonesia in 1996, compared with $5.35 billion in 1995. Of the total, Japan pledged $1.91 billion in 1996, compared with $2.14 billion in 1995.
Ginanjar said he visited Japan last week and met Japanese ministers covering the portfolios of finance, international trade and foreign affairs. He did not say whether the car issue was discussed.

Indonesia's national car policy gives PT Timor Putra Nasional, a firm headed by President Suharto's youngest son Hutomo Mandala Putra, tax and tariff breaks to produce a national car in association with Kia Motors Corp of South Korea.
Japan, the United States and the European Union have said the policy discriminates against other car manufacturers and have complained to the World Trade Organisation.
Indonesia has defended its policy by saying the national car programme aims to strengthen domestic industry.
